checklist.comments: Trip actually lasted 5.3 hours, but tracking cut out and eBird won't allow me to modify the effort.

obs.comments: The only duck of the day!  Seen very close to road from car 4.
One with no tail feathers at gathering place.
Remarkably low number for this area.

Most dowitchers at this time if year are of this species.  Adults have less extensive red in the underparts in the retained breeding plumage than Long-billed.  Markings toward the rear of the flanks are more spotted than chevroned.  Bill averages shorter, but there is much overlap.  Flatter backed with smaller chest and center of gravity closer to center.  Juveniles are very distinctive with warm brown tones to the breast and back.

One group was deemed to be of this species.  More hump-backed and big chested, often described as having swallowed a grapefruit.  Resting birds tend to sit with the body axis tilted up due to forward center of gravity.  Juveniles, which have not arrived yet, are much more uniform gray than juvenile Short-billed.

Some of these were in the distance and heat shimmer and left unidentified.  Given the time of year, they were likely mostly Short-billed.   Later in the fall and through the winter and spring, the Short-billed will move to brackish and salt water habitats near the coast, leaving the inland wetlands to the Long-billed Dowitchers.

Running count.  Extensive habitat and effort.  Skinny little mostly white shorebirds with needle-like bill and longish yellow legs.  Very active feeders, often spinning in the water or running circles in shallow waters.

Non-breeding plumage looks much like Lesser Yellowlegs.  Bill is thinner with a slight droop.  White line above eye.  Legs usually greenish yellow but can be yellow.  Never as yellow as yellowlegs.  Often associated with yellowlegs and dowitchers in migration and winter.

Tiny little shorebirds, smallest in the world.  Bill is thin with a slight decurve.  Legs are yellow, but can be covered in mud or darkened in the shade.  Always browner than other peep sandpipers.  Chest is solidly streaked with brown with a clean demarkation at the belly.
Looks like a giant Least Sandpiper.  Plumage pattern similar.  Much larger and plumper.  Males are larger than females.  Bill has pale spot near base.  Often found in sod fields.

Often difficult to separate from Western Sandpiper.  Bill is typically straight and somewhat peg like.  Paler than Western in breeding plumage.  At this time of year, the breeding plumage is somewhat worn making differences less distinct.
Several mud flats were covered in peeps that were too distant to ID in the time we had.
Rough count of shorebirds too far out for identification even to sub group.

Crazy numbers for this far inland.  This species make an annual pilgrimage to the Everglades Agricultural Area from breeding grounds on the coast to take advantage of the abundance of food made available by agricultural practices.

Not sure what these birds are doing inland at this time.  Possibly local breeders that wandered in with the Laughing Gulls to take advantage of the food.  Skimmers that were banded on the breeding grounds in New York have been seen on Lake Okeechobee as late as May.  It's unlikely that such late nesters would be back here this early.
Most were juveniles.  Probably nested somewhere near the coast, but could have been from some open ground or buildings nearby.

Counted over 120 in just one field.  Many more in flight and in other fields.  Rough running count kept throughout.  Extensive habitat and effort.

Most of the year, they are in nonbreeding plumage.  Very white with little black in the wings tips and almost no black on the head.  Several birds were retaining some black on the head from breeding plumage.  Thick head, neck, and bill with somewhat squarish tail, unlike most terns.  Perhaps it should be called Gull-like Tern.

Most have lost the entirely black underparts of breeding plumage.  Dark gray on the back and top of wings.  Black mark behind eye is retained in winter.  Smaller than the other terns with the exception of Least Tern.
Quite possibly an underestimate.  Attempted to keep a rough running count.  Draining of flooded fields has led to a concentration of abundant food resources.  Many or most of these were juveniles.
One flew over us.  Generally uncommon in the Everglades Agricultural Area in summer.  Quite common in winter.
One spied in the muck in the first big concentration of birds.  Almost the same color as the muck.
Saw a couple flying in the first leg of our journey.  Skinny looking compared to Black-crowned.  structure and voice very similar to Little Blue Heron.
Rough count of the many birds seen flying out along one of the roads.  Very chunky compared to Yellow-crowned.  Toes barely extend beyond tail tip in flight.
Big bulky white heron.  Legs pale.  Bill massive.  Bare skin extended behind eye.

One adult feeding in a field.  Second bird, likely a third year bird, further down.  Young bird had some white on the head with a dark stripe through the eye.  These birds are likely 3-4 years old.  It takes five years to mature.  Intermediate plumages are notoriously variable.
One reported near where the night-herons were flushing.  Most common buteo in Florida.
One was seen at the start.  Blue Jay is very local and uncommon in the Everglades Agricultural Area mainly due to the lack of trees.

Possibly more than this present.  At a few spots, multiples were passing around us.  Very white underneath with dark band on the breast.  Band can be difficult to observe in the field.  Very small with narrow body and wings compared to other swallows.  Solid brown above.

Small flock appeared as we ended the trip.  Most birds seen at this time of year are likely northern breeders making their way back to South America.  They will be completely gone from the continent by November, returning in early January.  Big body and broad wings help separate them from other swallows.

Only picked out a couple of these.  Narrow wings, brown above, but softer than Bank Swallow.  Brownish smudge on breast.  Wings narrow and swept back toward tail tip in flight, much like Barn Swallow.  Common here in winter.  Local breeder.

Most common migrant and breeding swallow in Florida.  Long formed tail is often not as prevalent ta this time when multiple immature birds are present and adults are molting tail feathers.  Generally reddish underparts but some worn birds or immatures can be nearly white.  Long narrow wings are swept back toward tail in flight.
One at the beginning, another along the way.  They are often found near any building in the area.  Most or all of them seem to have Black Rail calls in their repertoire.
Small group seen and heard at the beginning.
A few were seen flying out as we began our journey.
Small groups of often tailless birds seen.  Many individuals molt all of their tail feathers at once giving a no-tailed look for a few weeks at this time of year.
A couple were heard along the way.  Species is resident in the area, often heard singing in any vegetated moist area.
Heard one on the way out.  Usually we see a bunch of these, wherever there are trees, particularly willow trees.
Heard a couple along the way.  They are often found where there are hedgerows of trees and bushes along the canals.
